newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Despite problems E. Europe still offers good value.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Despite problems E. Europe still offers good value.

text.p: A currency crisis and growing current account deficits signalled a wake-up call to investors in Eastern Europe but economists in London say many countries in the region still offer sound prospects on an array of assets.

Continued reforms and fiscal austerity measures have assured investors that the political willingness on the part of governments to implement market-friendly policies continues to outweigh any associated risks, they add.

Economists say attractive investment opportunities can now be found in Bulgaria, Hungary, Romania and Russia --though they caution against investing in certain assets of the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Poland.
The big favourite among investors continues to be Russia, which has registered gains on certain assets of more than 50 percent this year.

And even though Russian assets have posted spectacular returns, economists say the horizon for the local currency GKO (government securities) market, the rouble and dollar-denominated debt still remains extremely favourable for the rest of the year.

"Anything that has even a vague Russian ring to it gets snapped up in the market because you get very attractive yields relative to other markets and the currency against the dollar has been very stable," said Nigel Rendell, emerging market economist at HSBC James Capel in London.
Rendell said declining inflation and stable currency should pave the way for further gains in the GKO market.

"The GKO has already performed pretty spectacularly with rates now down to 20 percent but I still think there is more improvement to come. With inflation dropping and the currency stable, we will see short rates coming down further," he said.
RUSSIA TOP CURRENCY CHOICE TOO
As for currency plays, economists say the Russian rouble remains the top pick.

"In Eastern Europe, the Russian rouble remains the most attractive investment. You are looking at 11 percent or more on U.S. dollar returns so it is far and away the most attractive currency in this part of the world," said Daniel McGovern, director of emerging markets in London at Merrill Lynch.
Russian dollar-denominated debt is also one of the best picks in that asset class despite delays in the closing of its debt restructuring plan with its commercial bank creditors.
"Russia stands out as a winner. Russia is still trading way too wide relative to credit quality," said Philip Poole, head of emerging markets research at ING Barings in London.
"I think Russia will tighten relative to the rest of the market by about 80 to 90 basis points by the end of the year and that is based on improving credit fundamentals," Poole added.
HUNGARY ANOTHER FAVOURITE
"Our favourite from a debt perspective or a currency perspective is Hungary in the short term because the currency is holding up reasonably well," said Rendell.

"There aren't any looming problems on the fiscal side or on the current account side but deficits are heading down fairly nicely at least for 1997," said Rendell, who noted a drop in the country's inflation rate would facilitate lower interest rates.
Poole agreed that Hungary continues to offer good value because of its stable environment and solid macroeconomic framework.
BULGARIA AND ROMANIA'S PROSPECTS IMPROVE
Bulgarian Brady debt also remains a favourite in its asset class because of the implementation of the currency board and the country's improving economic fundamentals.

McGovern said prospects for a smaller budget deficit, a stable currency and a possible current account surplus have Bulgaria poised for a credit rating upgrade and re-entry into the international capital markets by the end of the year or the beginning of 1998.
"Indeed, Bulgaria is really taking the right measures and we think there is high probability of a one, if not two, step upgrade. I think there is still significant upside in Bulgaria," he said.
While Romania is considered far more speculative than some of the countries, economists say potential upside movement remains both on the equity side as well as in eurobonds.
Expectations of a drop in the inflation rate, along with increased prospects for improvements in its fiscal account and current accounts should tempt investors to look to those markets, they said.
"I think that is a country which is starting to sort out its problems...so it's much more speculative grade but it is certainly one to watch over the 12 month horizon," said Rendell.
POLISH OUTLOOK CLOUDY, CZECH AND SLOVAK CURRENCIES RISKY
While economists were somewhat divided on Poland's investment outlook, they all agreed that the major concern is the country's growing account deficit.
"The current account numbers are very worrying. We are looking at a current account deficit of almost five percent of GDP and something close to 7-1/2 percent of GDP in 1998," said Rendell.
Costs related to the heavy flooding in Poland and increased political uncertainty ahead of parliamentary elections in September also make the country's dollar denominated assets less attractive.
"I would think Poland would continue to under-perform the rest of the market," said Poole.
As for the Czech Republic and Slovakia, market experts remain a bit more cautious. Economists say investors are likely to shun countries with current account deficits.
Though the devaluation of the Czech crown helped to improve the country's current account, economists think the government still needs to implement tough measures to get its fiscal balance in order.
"Without real strong fiscal measures, we think the Czech crown is still going to be a bit vulnerable," McGovern said.

"The government hasn't really offered anything in a way of a coherent economic strategy so people just want to keep away from the Czech Republic and that is true on the debt side and on the equity side," added Rendell.
Economists also remain pessimistic about Slovakia because of increased prospects for further erosion in their current account and trade balance.

"We think that in the next six months, there will probably be a significant devaluation to the Slovak currency, and given what we have seen recently with how quickly currencies could move it is simply too risky to be in the Slovak market," said McGovern.
